title: Paranormal Sutherlin: What local ghost hunters found in the dark at Danville Museum
excerpt: The voice booming in the Danville Museum was not coming from any of the people gathered in the room. “Pronounce it!” the male voice demanded.
content:
The voice booming in the Danville Museum was not coming from any of the people gathered in the room. “Pronounce it!” the male voice demanded.

To be clear, it was a recording presented on a video being played in the room.

To be more clear, it was a recording of a male voice caught during a late-night investigation in the Sutherlin mansion in Danville, by an all-woman crew of the Paranormal Research Society of Danville, at a time when there were no men present.

It was one of several surprising moments, captured on audio or video or photography and presented by the Society’s Team Lead Brandie Taylor on Friday night at the Danville Museum of Fine Arts and History, that could have convinced a skeptic there was something unusual afoot.

For those who spend their days (or nights) in the museum, housed in the Sutherlin mansion, they needed no convincing that there may be more inhabitants than one can see.

“You always feel like there’s somebody with you in this building,” said the museum board’s president John Harris.

Joe Wasek agreed. He described feeling a presence behind him watching him for several hours on a recent shift as he cleaned the building. “He was on my back for hours,” Wasek said. “I could feel him back there trying to make me uncomfortable.”

Museum Services Specialist Heidi Varga has had her own experiences in the building.

But what happens when you spend hours one summer evening really listening for those moments?

The tech and the tingle

Taylor presented a 40-minute video showing sights and sounds from the three-woman Society’s all-night investigation.

The team assembled on Friday, August 28. It took about an hour for the three Society members — Taylor, Hayley Watlington and Carlie Keller — to set up 7 static cameras, a mix of small motion-trigger cameras and trail cameras, as well as some of the tech of the ghost hunting trade, including a REM-POD (which lights up when there are changes in electromagnetic fields and ambient temperatures) and a LaserPro infrared thermometer. They performed their typical initial walk-through and determined their plan of action for the night, and began.

When the full moon rose over Danville at 8:07 p.m. shortly after sunset that evening, the team was in place, spending time in rooms, taking readings and measurements, and keeping all their senses keen.

They’d be there until about 1:30 on Saturday morning.

“While some locations seem to ramp up as the evening goes on, we have found the mansion does the opposite, having now been there twice,” Taylor said.

Things did indeed begin to happen. A camera tripod was knocked over with no visible cause, as recorded by another video camera. Voices caught on audio seemed to be conversations stuck in time, found only later as EVPs (electronic voice phenomena, where whispers, voices, or responses to the investigators questions are captured on audio recordings, even though they went unheard in the moment).

There were moments, notably in the cupola, where sensors were being activated constantly, lights were flashing, and it almost seemed like a social congenial atmosphere between all entities present.

It would take another month of sifting through the footage, photos and audio to find the most spine-tingling moments of that night.

“It’s very time-consuming,” Taylor wrote in an email to the Star-Tribune, “but rewarding when you do find pieces you cannot attribute to anything else, or those very rare class-A EVPs.”

One such EVP, combined with a striking image, may be telling a story about the mansion’s past that includes a well-known ghost and a potentially tragic situation.

The nurse and her grief

It was the time of the Spanish Flu.

Several buildings in Danville around 1918 and 1919, including the Sutherlin mansion, transitioned into makeshift hospitals staffed by volunteer nursing corps from the American Red Cross. Over 500 people died, according to Taylor’s research.

Taylor said it’s not known exactly what part of the mansion housed patients, but a woman in a nurse’s uniform had been seen on the second floor by numerous museum visitors to the Danville Museum.

She didn’t know it when she was taking photographs of a room on the second floor that she’d be yet another person to get a glimpse of the nurse, this time as she examined the photographs in September.

In the image a fuzzy figure appears to be standing by the fireplace. As Taylor and her team worked with the photograph, she realized she was looking at the nurse. Their debunking process made them more certain of what they were seeing. “The more that I tried to rule her out, the more clear certain things came to me,” Taylor said. “Like her hat is so divine. The little pin on her hat.”

In September they also heard the audio of the male voice, captured on the trail cam, saying, “Pronounce it.”

“The ‘Pronounce it’ EVP occurred around the same time that I took the nurse photo,” Taylor said.

The two phenomena came together for her. The male voice could have been a doctor instructing someone to pronounce a patient dead. “So in that moment, they have lost somebody.” As a practicing nurse herself for the last 16 years, Taylor knows the trauma of losing a patient. “To capture that moment is just crazy for me personally.” She doesn’t think the nurse herself died in the building, but that perhaps experiencing that specific death “could leave a mark” on her that would result in a “residual event” — her oft-noticed presence in the building.

“I was completely unaware at the time that I had captured one of the most prominent photos I think I've ever taken, and this is with nearly a decade of doing this, coupled with the EVP of what sounds to be a male saying pronounce it. Was this the residual energy from when this particular building used to be a makeshift flu hospital?”

The figure in the image seems to be both behind and above a glass case in the room, so not a simple case of an odd reflection, which would have appeared consistently in photos. “I had a photo from directly after that when she was not there,” Taylor told the audience Friday. The photo is posted on the Paranormal Research Society of Danville’s Facebook page.

‘It’s different here’

Several people at the event said that. Beyond the photos and videos and EVPs and blinking REM-PODs, the feeling at the mansion was special to them as human beings perceiving the space around them, and the site appears very active for those interested in the paranormal. Maybe it’s because the paranormal team is local and these presences appreciate that. Maybe it’s because the mansion is at the geographic pinnacle of the city, and the cupola is at the pinnacle of the mansion, as if all human emotions climbed their way up the hill and through the building, to the highest point of man-made presence, before moving on.

Or not quite moving on, it seems.

Lights and sensors were triggered almost constantly in the cupola in what Taylor called one of the most active scenes she’d encountered anywhere.

Society member Carlie Keller said it felt like people were constantly coming up and down the steps for their smoke break.

Harris said about the cupola, “It will draw you there. After you know it’s there, it draws you there. There’s a time of year in the late fall and early spring, there’s an energy there that just draws you up there for some reason.”

After the event, Joe Wosak was getting ready to do some cleaning.

He wasn’t scared, he said. “Every now and then I might get a few chills. But you know, we’ve seen and heard a lot of things here.”

For those who missed this event, another investigative team, The Heritage Hunters, performed their own investigation of the mansion, and will show their findings on Friday, Oct. 23 at 6:00 p.m. at the Danville Museum. Tickets are $10 at the door, and wine and other beverages will be available for purchase.
